content: Theth is a remote village in the northern Albanian Alps, set in a glacial valley inside Theth National Park. Most visitors reach it by a winding mountain road from Shkodër, about a 3 to 4 hour drive, or on the popular day hike from Valbona over the Valbona Pass.

Accommodation in Theth is mostly family-run guesthouses offering half-board with home-cooked meals. Book ahead in July and August, when the village fills with hikers heading to the Blue Eye of Theth and the Grunas waterfall.

Gjirokastër Castle dominates the hilltop above the old town and is one of the largest fortresses in Albania. Inside you will find a Cold War era US Air Force jet and the National Weapons Museum; the ramparts give sweeping views over the stone-roofed Ottoman houses below.

Gjirokastër is a UNESCO-listed city of stone in southern Albania, famous for its steep cobbled bazaar and distinctive slate-roofed tower houses. It is roughly an hour's drive from the Greek border and a common stop between Sarandë and Berat.

Berat is known as the city of a thousand windows for the tiered Ottoman houses climbing the slopes of the Mangalem and Gorica quarters. The UNESCO-protected old town sits beneath Berat Castle, which is still inhabited today.

Berat Castle (Kalaja) is a rare living fortress where families still live inside its walls among Byzantine churches and the Onufri icon museum. Entry to the castle grounds is free, and the climb up from the old town takes about twenty minutes.

The Blue Eye (Syri i Kaltër) is a natural spring near Sarandë where deep blue water bubbles up from a pool of unknown depth. It is a short detour off the road between Sarandë and Gjirokastër; swimming is discouraged because the water is icy and very deep.

Furgons are shared minibuses and the backbone of Albanian public transport. They do not run on fixed timetables; they leave when full, and you pay the driver in cash (lek). For routes like Tirana to Berat or Sarandë, ask locals where the furgons depart, as stops are often informal.

The Llogara Pass climbs to around 1,000 metres over the Ceraunian Mountains, with the road switchbacking down toward the Riviera. The viewpoint at the top looks straight down onto the coast at Dhërmi and Palasë; it is one of the most dramatic drives in Albania.
Sarandë is a busy seaside town on the Albanian Riviera and a gateway to Ksamil's beaches and the ancient ruins of Butrint. Ferries connect it to Corfu in under an hour during summer.

Tirana, the capital, centres on Skanderbeg Square, ringed by the colourful façades of the old government buildings, the National History Museum, and the Et'hem Bey Mosque. The Blloku district is the hub for cafés and nightlife.
Ksamil is a small resort south of Sarandë known for white-sand coves and shallow turquoise water dotted with tiny islets you can swim out to. It gets very crowded in August.

Rozafa Castle stands on a rocky hill where the Buna and Drin rivers meet, just outside Shkodër in the far north. It is bound up with the legend of a young woman immured in its walls so the fortress would stop collapsing, and the ramparts look out over Lake Shkodër and the plain below.

Krujë Castle was the stronghold of Skanderbeg, Albania's national hero, during his fifteenth-century resistance to the Ottomans. Inside the walls the Skanderbeg Museum tells that story, and the restored old bazaar just below the gate sells antiques, carpets, and traditional crafts.

Petrelë Castle is a small Byzantine-era fortress on a wooded hill about twenty minutes south of Tirana. These days it is best known for the panoramic terrace restaurant inside its walls, making it an easy half-day escape from the capital with wide views over the Erzen valley.

Dhërmi is one of the best-known beaches on the Albanian Riviera, a long pebble bay below the Llogara Pass with clear water and a row of summer beach clubs. The whitewashed old village climbs the hillside above, while the seafront fills with music and crowds in high season.

Himarë is a coastal town on the Riviera with a cluster of pebble beaches such as Livadhi and Spille, a small harbour, and a Greek-speaking community that keeps its own dialect. A ruined castle and the quiet upper village sit on the slopes behind the modern seafront.

Borsh has the longest beach on the Albanian Riviera, a wide stretch of pebble and shingle running for several kilometres beneath a hillside of olive groves. It stays quieter and less built-up than Dhërmi or Ksamil, with a medieval castle above and cold freshwater streams reaching the sea.

Jale is a small cove between Vuno and Himarë that has become the Riviera's main party beach, packed with young crowds, beach bars, and summer music camps. The bay itself is a sheltered crescent of pebbles with a couple of campsites tucked in behind it.

The Blue Eye of Theth is a vivid turquoise pool fed by an icy mountain stream, reached on a two to three hour walk up the valley from Theth village in the northern Alps. The water stays freezing cold all year, and the trail passes through beech forest and small wooden footbridges.

The Grunas Waterfall drops around thirty metres down a rock face a short hike south of Theth village, on the way toward the Grunas canyon. It is one of the gentlest walks in the valley, under an hour each way, and the spray keeps the pool at its base cold even in midsummer.

The Bogova Waterfall sits above the village of Bogovë in the Tomorr mountains east of Berat, reached by a forest trail that follows a cold stream. The falls feed a small natural pool that draws people for a bracing summer swim, and the surrounding slopes are protected parkland.

Lake Ohrid is one of the oldest and deepest lakes in Europe, shared between Albania and North Macedonia and protected by UNESCO for its rare endemic life. On the Albanian shore the town of Pogradec is the main base, known for its lakeside promenade and the prized koran trout.

The Koman Ferry threads through a flooded river canyon on Lake Koman, a three-hour boat ride often likened to a fjord, with sheer cliffs rising straight from the green water. Most travellers take it as the scenic link between Shkodër and Valbona, loading cars and minibuses onto the deck at the Koman dam.

Valbona is an alpine village in the Valbona Valley National Park in the far north, ringed by the jagged peaks of the Albanian Alps. It is the other end of the classic day hike over the pass from Theth, and family-run guesthouses along the river valley fill with trekkers through the summer.

Shkodër is the cultural capital of the north and the main gateway to the Alps and the Koman Ferry. Its pedestrian Kolë Idromeno street, the Marubi photography museum, and bike-friendly streets lead out to Lake Shkodër, the largest lake in the Balkans.

Korçë is the main city of the southeast, known for its restored Old Bazaar, the National Museum of Medieval Art, and a tradition of guitar serenades. It is home to the country's oldest brewery, and its higher altitude brings real snow in winter.

Durrës is Albania's main port and second-largest city, on the Adriatic just west of Tirana. A huge Roman amphitheatre sits in the middle of town, and a long sandy beach strip runs south toward Golem, packed with Albanian holidaymakers in summer.

Vlorë is the port city where Albania declared its independence in 1912, remembered at Flag Square and the Independence Monument. It sits where the Adriatic meets the Ionian and is the northern starting point of the Riviera coast road that climbs over the Llogara Pass.

Butrint is a UNESCO World Heritage archaeological park on a wooded peninsula south of Sarandë, layered with Greek, Roman, Byzantine, and Venetian remains. Its highlights include the Greek theatre, the baptistery with its mosaic floor, the Lion Gate, and a triangular Venetian fortress above the lagoon.
